speechtext: BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries') moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 152) respecting signal dues at Halifax.
Explain.

The object of the Bill is to permit vessels having a tonnage of less than 150 tons to come into the harbour at Halifax without being obliged to pay what we call signal dues. There is a signal station at Halifax for the purpose of signalling vessels, but only those having a larger tonnage than 150 tons are signalled. We think that under these circumstances all vessels which are not signalled when they come into the harbour should not be obliged to pay the dues. The object of the Bill is for the purpose of abolishing dues in so far as these vessels are concerned.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The present prohibition of methyl alcohol is confined to articles intended for internal use. We add subsection 2 to section 206, and we do this in consequence of the large number of fatalities that have occurred throughout the country by the use, ignorantly no doubt, of methyl alcohol. We have taken the opportunity of this amendment of the Inland Revenue Act to make this change. We purpose-and I think there is a clause later on -to provide that the manufacturers of wood alcohol shall be licensed. This is done for the purpose of bringing them under the jurisdiction and control of the Department of Inland Revenue. We will charge the mere nominal fee of $1 for a license and will require them to label the barrels and receptacles in which wood alcohol is placed with the word ' Poison.' We think this is in the interest of the public and that it will safeguard the people from the use, ignorantly or otherwise, of wood alcohol.

What steps, if any, has the minister taken looking to remedy the complaint that has been made concerning the excessive cost of this alcohol which is the basis of so many preparations ? I think we had a discussion in the House a year or two ago with reference to it, and the general idea was that the price of this material was very high compared with the price in the United States, where they have, by improved processes and by changes in the law, greatly reduced the cost of alcohol. I think the minister stated that he was making experiments in the same direction. I have letters in my hand setting forth the disability under which the druggists labour on this account. I would like the minister, if he can, to give a brief statement of what he is doing in that respect Mr. TEMPLEMAN.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The question of providing denatured alcohol, as it is sometimes called, or methylated spirits, at cheap rates has been engaging the attention of the Department of Inland Revenue for a year or two. The department makes methylated spirits. It has kept this manufacture in its control for years for the purpose of safeguarding the revenue. The methylated spirits placed upon the market of Canada for many years, has been mostly of two grades, one being 50 per cent wood alcohol and 50 per cent grain alcohol, and the other being 25 per cent wood alcohol and 75 per cent grain alcohol. The cost of the grain alcohol as purchased by the department from distillers has been about 41 or 42 cents per gallon, at the strength used for methylated spirits. Up to the present time the cost of wood alcohol to the department has been $1.29 per gallon. We have put these two-grades of methylated spirits on the market for a number of years at $1.10 per gallon and $1.25, the latter being the price of alcohol containing 50 per cent wood alcohol. During the past year we have reduced these prices until at the present time we sell No. 1 grade at 70 cents and No. 2 grade at 80 cents. We have been experimenting in the laboratory with spirits to see if we could not properly safeguard the revenue by using a smaller percentage of wood alcohol, and the consequence is that we have put on the market an alcohol at 65 cents per gallon. Now I have said that the price of wood alcohol up to the period of the termination of the last contract was $1.29 per bulk gallon. During the last year the price of wood alcohol, particularly in the United States, has decreased very materially. In the United States, my hon. friend must remember, until one year ago, the manufacturers had to use wood alcohol pure and simple, or if they used ethyl alcohol they had to pay the duty. Canada has been far in advance of the United States for many years in this respect; but two-years ago the United States Congress passed a law authorizing licenses to distillers and others to take alcohol out of bond and denature it. They have done so, and they are placing on the market to-day a denatured alcohol of which about 90 per cent is grain alcohol and 10 per cent wood alcohol, and they are selling it at 40 eents a wine gallon, which, being one-fifth or one-sixth less in bulk than the imperial gallon, is after all not as cheap as one would imagine. At the price at which the department will be able henceforth to purchase wood alcohol, the market price in Canada to-day being, I think, something like 50 cents and upward, acording to grade, the reduction the department will make in the present price wilt be very material; and I think that, even with the disadvantages under which we labour in Canada of making cheap grain alcohol as compared with the distillers of the United States, we will be able to put on the

market before long a denatured alcohol at prices very little above those In the United States. Of the two grades of methylated spirits placed upon the market by the department for a long time, No. 1, with 75 per cent of grain alcohol, has been sold to manufacturers and others who enter into a bond that it shall be used only in their business and not be sold or transferred to others The other grade, No. 2, was sold to the public at large without any restriction whatever, the department feeling confident that an alcohol containing 50 per cent of wood alcohol was a perfectly safe article to place on the market so far as the revenue was concerned. This, Mr. Chairman, is the situation at the present time. We hope in the future to make considerable progress in reducing the price of methylated spirits. Up to the time that we could procure a cheap wood alcohol, after the termination of our contract, no effort has been made to remove the cost of denaturing, which I think is quite feasible. The wood alcohol now mixed by the department is all brought to Ottawa, upon which freight has to be paid, and I think it will be possible considerably to, reduce the cost of denaturing before long.
Where does the minister get his wood alcohol? Is any of it made in Canada?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is all made in Canada. .
I mean is any of it made in Canada that is not made under the supervision of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is no supervision, we are taking that power now. Wood alcohol, as a substance by itself, is made by the manufacturers of charcoal and others ; it is free to any person to make it and place it on the market. We have no restriction over its manufacture. We now propose to take control over the manufacture of alcohol simply for the purpose of safeguarding the lives of people by compelling the manufacturers to put labels on every vessel to show that the contents are wood alcohol, because it is very often taken for something else.
Is the disability under which Canada rests as regards the superfluity of grain, the only disability that makes the comparison so much against us as regards the United States ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I think the disability as compared with the alcohol produced in certain districts of the United States is considerable. In the first place, I think the corn imported into Canada comes directly from the corn producing belt and has to pay freight. There is, I think, a small tax, something like seven and a half cents per bushel, on corn used in the production of alcohol. The distillers in the United States are located in districts where corn is grown
in large quantities, and where coal for fuel is practically at their very door. It is a question whether, if we attempted to produce a cheap denatured alcohol, we would be able to remove that disability, so far as concerns alcohol used for denaturing purposes. That might be practicable without at all affecting the revenue or changing the taxes. There are many disabilities but these are probably the principal ones. The price of coal is another. When I asked distillers why they could not sell alcohol as cheaply as it is sold in the United States, they said that in southern Illinois, I think Peoria is the centre, they are near the corn fields and the coal fields and have facilities for producing alcohol at a very low' price.
What is the difference in the cost at the present time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot give that information exactly. We are at present very much handicapped by reason of the excessive price of wood alcohol. I look forward hopefully to the possibility of placing denatured alcohol on the market in Canada at a considerably reduced price. At the same time the great object the people have in mind is a denatured alcohol that may be used for fuel, light or motive purposes. I give no opinion as to the possibility of that. The use of alcohol in competing with gasoline or petroleum is not likely to become general in Canada for some time to come. While it may be possible to produce alcohol in Canada much more cheaply than at present, it would have to be produced at one-half the price of to-day before it could be sold in competition with gasoline and petroleum.

What struck me was the possibility of people generally manufacturing their own alcohol and thus getting an extremely cheap motive power. I read some articles with reference to this in the United States and they seemed to have overcome the difficulty in regard to revenue and were able to produce a wonderfully cheap article for motive power and other industrial uses. I would like the minister to state whether this has been successfully carried out in the United States, and if so, why Canada could not do the same thing. My recollection is that they proposed to make the alcohol out of farm refuse of. different kinds w'hich is now practically wasted, but which is claimed under proper education could be converted into alcohol by farmers themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The officials of the department have been in communication with the officials of the department in Washington with respect to the operation of their law, and their information is that it has not been successful in regard to the distillation of alcohol by farmers. All the denatured alcohol put on the market in the United States in the last twelve months

'has been from the grain distillers. It was expected that there would be such a thing as agricultural distilleries, that any farmer might have a license, might have a small still, and under the supervision of excise officers distil his own alcohol from corn stalks or other similar waste products of the farm. However, this has not been accomplished in the United States. Our department have watched it with interest; we would very much like to have them work out this problem successfully before venturing along a line in which there is serious danger to the revenue unless the work is carried out under the closest supervision.

I think I recollect a speech by the hon. member for East Kent (Mr. Gordon) on this subject some two or three years ago, and I was rather impressed with what he said with respect to the progress which Germany has made in the production of this article for purposes such as the hon. member has alluded to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Germany is always pointed to as the country that has succeeded in producing denatured alcohol for fuel purposes, for driving motors, &c. A year ago, when the question was before the House, I read some of the reports in regard to the success of this alcohol in Germany, including the report prepared by a commission of the imperial parliament to investigate this question in regard to the effect of tax-paying alcohol on the industries of Great Britain as compared with the freer alcohol of Germany. I learned then, and I believe It is the fact, that Germany encourages by a subsidy the production of alcohol on the farm. Germany also imposes a tax upon petroleum. It encourages the production of alcohol by farmers to the extent of 6 cents or 7 cents a gallon. I do not think that policy would be acceptable in Canada. Then Germany has very cheap labour. The inauguration of the alcohol industry in Germany was due to agrarian politics. There were very large areas of poor land and many poor people, and they were encouraged to go on these lands to grow potatoes and manufacture alcohol. It was not altogether a question of producing cheap fuel, it had something to do with the settlement of poor lands in Saxony and other provinces of Germany. A large quantity of alcohol is used in Germany for fuel and light purposes, which is made from potatoes. I do not think we desire conditions in this country which would enable us to obtain the same measure of cheap alcohol ; I understand that unless our farmers are prepared to grow potatoes at a price of about 10 cents or 12 cents a bushel they will not be able to produce alcohol to compete with the present price of petroleum and gasoline in Canada.

I wish to call attention to the situation that is created in that way. Perhaps I might bring that out by reading Mr. TEMPLEMAN.

There is a matter of very considerable interest to ourselves

-well as to the drug trade generally that has already or will in the very near future be brought to the attention of the House . . . . and that is the question of the exorbitant prices we are obliged to pay for alcohol for use in the arts. The manufacturers are obliged to keep this article in stock for three years in order to comply with the regulations.. We consider this absolutely unnecessary when the alcohol is used for manufacturing purposes, and this fact adds practically 50 per cent to the actual cost of the spirit, without, of course, considering the question of government duty.
That is an assertion which is worthy of some consideration. They make the flat statement that it is not necessary to keep this alcohol for three years maturing in order to prepare it for use in the manufactures. If it is a fact that it need not be kept so long there should be a great reduction in price. Whether that is practicable or not is a question which remains for the minister to consider.
A denatured alcohol is manufactured and sold in the United States at 39 cents per gallon which illustrates the fact that a spirit can be manufactured and sold, if there were no duty to pay and it had not to be kept for three years, at from 40 to 50 cents per gallon, imperial measure, with a very good profit. Of course, the government duty is placed high enough so as to prevent any spirit being imported.
In the general policy of the country, which is to aid and enlarge manufacturing interests as greatly as possible, here is one manufacturing interest which, upon such a statement of the case, seems to be placed at a disadvantage in its competition with respect to articles coming from other countries and the manufacturers of which have a cheaper basic article to commence with. Has the minister looked into the point as to whether it is necessary to keep alcohol maturing so long for this purpose ? If it is not, of course, there may be some cheapening in that respect. It does seem as though they state, prirna facie, a case which is worthy of consideration. The department gets out a great many bulletins, some of which are not very interesting. It would really be interesting if the officers of the department would look into the processes which have been started in other countries and for which great claims have been made, and once in a while summarizing the results of these experiments in other countries. For instance, it would be very interesting if they would summarize In a short bulletin the results of the experiments which have been made in this line and show the

relative progress as between ourselves and other countries which may set the people thinking, and which may be a spur to inventive genius outside of the Department of Inland Revenue as to the ways and means by which some similar effects may be produced in this country. But, I would ask the minister in reference to these two points that are referred to here, first, as to the cost of alcohol for manufacturing purposes.
'Mr. TEMPLEMAN. I think my hon. friend is probably mixing up two things. Denatured alcohol or methylated spirits is used for manufacturing purposes. It may be used if we can get it cheaply enough, for fuel and light, for driving motors and things of that kind. But what my hon. friend refers to is pure grain alcohol-

Yes, that is right.
Mr. TEMPLUMAN -for chemical purposes. An order in council was passed years ago permitting the use of grain alcohol by paying fifteen cents a gallon for the manufacture of anything in the process of manufacture of which the alcohol was destroyed or was so changed that it could not be recovered. That is the law to-day. When the motion of my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) was up for discussion the other day, the question arose as to whether we could not permit the manufacture of several other articles, chloroform being one, and I submitted the proposition to the chemist of the department. I am advised that he has made a report in which he says that some of the articles that it is proposed to manufacture in Canada might be permitted to be manufactured with perfect safety to the revenue, but that there are several others that my hon. friend from Winnipeg thought that we might manufacture with perfect safety to the revenue that I am advised could not be so manufactured. We cannot permit grain alcohol to go into the possession of the manufacturing druggists of the country to be manufactured, unless in the process of manufacture the alcohol is either destroyed or so changed that it is worthless and cannot be recovered. To that extent only can we encourage manufactures that require alcohol. So long as they change the alcohol and so long as it cannot be restored to its original character as being a potable article, the department will permit the use of alcohol for paying fifteen cents a gallon.
That might be extended beyond what it has been.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, I am advised that it might be extended to several important articles. But, the complaint made by the writer of the letter to my hon. friend that grain alcohol has to be kept for three years in the warehouse without being sold under this clause is entirely wrong.
Under that clause probably it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is quite possible under this clause for any manufacturer to get alcohol out of the warehouse the day after it is manufactured. There is no need of maturing it for three years. Possibly the writer of the letter only takes alcohol that has been three years maturing and for which he pays $1.90 a gallon as many of the druggists throughout the country do.
On section 8,-application for license to manufacture tobacco.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is no change in this clause, except that the three last lines of the present Act are dropped.
On section 9

New section 275-fee for license

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Under the law as It is now there are three different licenses, with fees of $50, $65 and $75 respectively. It is proposed that in future there shall be but one license, with a fee of $50.
On section 10-New section 278-notices; to be posted up in tobacco manufactories-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The change in the notice is due to the fact that there will be but one license, as there will be no question whether the tobacco is imported or Canadian.
On section 11-New section 279-duties of excise on tobacco.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This clause provides for the changes made in the duties. On manufactured tobaccos and snuffs, the duty is to be 5 cents a pound. At present the duty on snuff is 25 cents a pound.
Does the duty of 5 cents a pound apply to the ordinary twist which the tobacco grower sells to the manufacturer ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

In the province of
Quebec, there has been no tax on twist.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There has always been a tax. There is no change in that respect.
There is no duty on the tobacco that a man grows for his own use.
[DOT] Do I understand that a man is not liable for duty on what he manufactures for his own use ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The law for years has provided in section 325 that a man may manufacture for the use of himself and his family to the extent of thirty pounds in a year, without paying duty.
Is the department able-to keep track of that fairly well ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think so. As far as my knowledge goes there has been no abuse of that provision.
Does the minister ever find some abnormally large families ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Occasionally, especially in the province of Quebec.
On subsection (g)-duty on cigarettes-
Is there any change in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The duty is changed from $3 to $2.40 per thousand.

I would like to ask the minister, now that he is changing the regulations regarding the manufacture of tobacco, cigars and cigarettes, what the policy of the government is in respect to the cigarette question. I think this would be a favourable opportunity for the government to state their position, in view of the fact that the House some time ago adopted a resolution in favour of prohibiting the manufacture, importation and sale of cigarettes in any part of Canada. I have been waiting for the government to make some pronouncement, and I expected, when this Bill was introduced the government would be -prepared to announce their policy. I am quite anxious to know how far the government will disregard the votes of the people's representatives on this question, more especially in view of the fact that some members of the cabinet expressed themselves in the House in favour of it. I am quite sure that the hon. minister, in the preparation of this Bill, gave some consideration to this question and has not disregarded entirely the wishes of the people as expressed in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This Bill is simply for the purpose of changing slightly the method of collecting duties on tobacco and cigars, and therefore is not one on which we can properly discuss the policy of prohibiting the use of cigarettes.
You could introduce a clause in this Bill providing that in future no cigarettes may be manufactured or sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am rather sympathetic with regard t!o the discouragement of the use of cigarettes by our youth, and I believe that something ought to be done on that line by means of an amendment to the Criminal Code. I am not quite prepared to admit that the prohibition of the manufacture and sale of cigarettes would be the proper course. At any rate this is not a Bill on which we can discuss that question.

That is a very nice statement from my hon. friend the minister, but the people would rather have the minister do something practical to carry out their wishes than merely express sympathy. I Mr. FOSTER.
would draw his attention to a letter complimenting the government for granting rather special favours to the cigarette manufacturers in Canada rather than carry out the wishes of the people's representatives. As a result of the discussion in the House a short time ago, a cigarette manufacturer in Montreal sent his compliments to each member of the House with a box of cigarettes and a letter.
I did not get any.
That is another grievance for you.

The letter is as follows : Montreal, Canada, March 17, 1908.
J. W. Daniel. Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-We take the liberty of transmitting to you to-day a sample of our cigarettes. We have factories established at London, England; Cairo, Egypt, and New York. This sample is from our new Canadian factory in this city and which we are enabled to operate satisfactorily, due alone to this legislation of your honourable House which abolished the sale contract system of the Tobacco Trust. While the tobacco trade do not as yet altogether realize the freedom of trading you have extended by your Act, and while a certain detrimental fear still exists, due to the past and present conduct of the monopoly, a better state of trading prevails and an independent house can operate in this market.
We wish to acknowledge the fact to-day, with thanks.
Respectfully yours,
PHILIP MORRIS & COMPANY, Limited,
Henry Miles, President.
That is not the result of this legislation.

I think that on this question of cigarette smoking, we all sympathize with the idea expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) so far as the youth of our land are concerned. It is very unfortunate that young people are induced to smoke cigarettes. I think some legislation should be passed for the purpose of doing away with this evil as far as possible, and I would agree with my hon. friend in supporting any legislation wisely designed to that end. The Bill now before us is not for the purpose of legislating in that way, but has to do with the raising of the public revenue. In some respects, the duty on cigarettes has been increased, which, I take it, is a step in the direction that my hon. friend wishes. I sympathize strongly with the idea that we should have legislation to prohibit young people from smoking cigarettes, and merchants and dealers from selling cigarettes to such people.
Was this increase in the duty made with the idea of mitigating the [DOT]evil ?
I say the duty was increased, and this would tend to decrease the consumption.
Was that the purpose in *the mind of the government when the duty was decreased?
The main purpose was to equalize the revenue.

I thought that from what the minister said-and I do not see why he should say it unless it had that bearing- that the government had the idea of mitigating to some extent this bad practice of using cigarettes when it increased the duty. It appears, however, that this was merely a 200
word that escaped the minister's lips, and that it did not express an idea which was in the mind of the government or of the Minister of Inland Revenue when the duties were increased. It might be better if we did not make these assertions unless we meant them, as they might be interpreted by those outside in a wrong way. I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Brodeur) would be the last man in this House to put it in that way to get the benefit of a wrong interpretation of the object in view in fixing this duty. I think we ought to have more from the government on this subject than we have had. It seems that we have no other opportunity. I was not present when the resolution of my hon. friend from Feel (Mr. Blain) was moved and debated. Had I been here I would have supported him as I did on a former occasion. While there was a sympathetic reception of that resolution on both sides of the House, the resolution seems to have been side-tracked by one of the devices well known to parliamentary practice and now stands where it is impossible, as I understand it, to recover it during the present session. I think my hon. friend from Peel is quite within his rights, when a chance opportunity comes in the form of legislation on this very subject, to ask the government to say what they would have said if this discussion had been allowed its course and had come to a conclusion either by a vote or by a statement made by the government and withdrawal of the motion if the statement were satisfactory. Really, this matter does merit consideration on our part. I do not suppose that you could find a single educationalist in the country who would not tell you that there is scarcely any more deleterious agent at work in depreciating and weakening the intellect of the youth of our country than this insidious habit of cigarette smoking. I think that educationalists will agree with that and that they are more and more pressing forward this idea. I do not suppose you will find a reputable physician who will stake his reputation on the statement that cigarette smoking is beneficial to the health of the young-or of anybody, though the grown person, with fibres set and full growth attained, might smoke cigarettes without receiving any very great injury. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brodeur) will know that the highest military authorities in Germany and Great Britain have sounded a note of warning concerning the effect of cigarette smoking upon the morale and upon the physicial fibre of the militia and soldiery of their respective countries. In fact, cigarette smoking cannot be proven to be beneficial in any way, and, from all these sources of which I have spoken, we have warnings as to its deleterious effects. Now we spend a lot of money to bring desirable immigrants to this country in order that we may increase the population of Canada. It seems to me we ought to very seriously consider whether we can keep



those that are born in our country and grow them up to the best stature of manhood and womanhood by removing deleterious agencies such as the cigarette is acknowledged to be. Why should we, on the one hand, spend money to bring in foreign adults to add to our population, and, on the other hand, allow an influence of this kind to neutralize our efforts by injuring those born in our midst? The matter of revenue is something, but revenue cannot be compared in importance for a moment with the health and wellbeing of the people. The Prime Minister {Sir Wilfrid Laurier) knows, from the deputations that have waited upon him-and also, no doubt, a great deal of correspondence has reached him-that there is a very widespread interest in this matter throughout the country. I think it may be stated that the best people of Canada are in favour of mitigating as far as possible, and, if possible, prohibiting, this practice in our country. It would be a great help if the Prime Minister could translate his sympathies and that of his friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) into words that would be hopeful and helpful to the important section of the population which is trying to minimize these evils. I think this is a golden opportunity for a word of sympathy if nothing further can be had.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will approach this 'question upon the very lines stated by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) himself. But, I may preface what I have to say on this occasion by stating that in this matter I am absolutely disinterested. I do not use tobacco in any form. If I were to follow my own inclination, I would have no hesitation in prohibiting cigarettes, cigars, smoking tobacco and chewing tobacco as well. But that would be going further perhaps, than would be acceptable to the great majority of this people. Coming to the observations of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) he has stated that this is a golden opportunity for the government to state their policy on the question brought before the House by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) in his resolution to prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes throughout the length and breadth of the land. This is no opportunity at all, I may say, by the way. This Bill is for the purpose of readjusting the excise duties upon tobacco, and has absolutely no connection with the question that has now been brought before the House, the question that was discussed a few days ago on the motion of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain).
The hon. gentleman asked what opinion I entertained on the subject. When the debate took place some time ago I stated my own view, and I have stated it before. I agree with the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Foster) that the use of cigarettes by boys is injurious, that is admitted, and seems to be beyond doubt. He has stated Mr. FOSTER.
also that the use of tobacco or cigarettes by mature men is innoxious. Now if this form of tobacco is injurious to the mature youth but is not noxious to the mature man, would my hon. friend conclude that we should prohibit the use of tobacco to the mature man as well as to the youth? I do not think that would be logical. If the use of cigarettes or tobacco in any form is innoxious to the mature man what reason can there be for depriving him of that comfort? Tobacco as has been very often said, is the luxury of the poor man. Does the hon. gentleman contend that under such circumstances we should deprive him from the use of tobacco, that we should stop its use not only to the person whom it injures but also the person whom it does not injure? I think the remedy suggested by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) is too radical, it goes too far, because he wants to prohibit the use of tobacco to a class of people whom it does not injure.
Keep in view the fact that it is only cigarettes, not tobacco or cigars, that I propose to prohibit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Exactly, and I take the view of the hon. member for Toronto, that cigarettes, while they are injurious to the mature youth, are absolutely innoxious to the mature man.

My right hon. friend has misunderstood me. I did not say, at least I did not mean to say that the smoking of cigarettes was innoxious to the mature man; my own opinion is that it is noxious instead of being innoxious. What I said was that it had less effect upon the mature man than upon a younger person. But I do not subscribe to the idea that the smoking of cigarettes is altogether innoxious to the mature man ; in fact my citing the opinions of military men as to the harmful effects of cigarettes upon soldiers, was proof that I took the ground that they were noxious and harmful to men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps I misunderstood my hon. friend, but I gathered that much from the way he emphasized the fact that the use of the cigarette was not so harmful to a man whose muscles were knit and set as it was to a mature youth, and I thought he had come to the conclusion that it was innoxious to the mature man. At all events, so far as I am concerned, I cannot see how tobacco in one form can be more injurious than in another form. I have never heard any reasoning that convinced me that tobacco used in a paper envelope is more noxious than tobacco used without any wrapper at all, for instance, when used in a pipe. The great mischief which I see in the cigarette is its cheapness. When I was a youngster, if a boy had five cents he invested it in candy ; but in these days when a boy has five cents

he goes and buys a package of cigarettes. This is the great mischief in the use of tobacco. Does the hon. gentleman think that tobacco itself, which is certainly injurious to the mature youth, whether in the form of cigarettes, cigars or pipe tobacco, should not be allowed to the mature man ? For my part I believe that tobacco 4n any form is dangerous to the mature boy and should not be allowed. But does my hon. friend believe that there is more danger in the use of tobacco in the shape of a cigarette than in any other form ?
To the boy, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why to the boy than to the man? Does the hon. gentleman believe that if a boy smokes a cigar the effect will not be the same as when he smokes a cigarette?
He will not be so prone to smoke a pipe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Exactly. As I said the peculiar danger of the cigarette was its cheapness. I must say-I have said it elsewhere to a deputation of ladies who came to interview me upon the subject- that it grates upon my feelings when walking the streets of a city to see a boy with a cigarette in his mouth, and I am tempted, like my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson),- to take the cigarette away and to say : My boy, you should not do that. In fact a few months ago, in the city of Quebec, I met a little lad with a cigarette in his mouth, and I took it away from him and said : My little fellow, you should not do that.
What did the boy say?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that the boy was rebellious to my good advice. But I repeat the cigarette is a form of tobacco which is undoubtedly injurious to the boy, but which is perfectly innoxious to the man. My hon. friend from Toronto will not say that a cigarette is any more injurious to a man than a pipe, and he wants to take away from the man the privilege of smoking cigarettes in order that he may preserve the boy from smoking them. That seems to be going too far. I believe there is legislation in every province forbidding or prohibiting the sale of cigarettes to boys; there is legislation in every province preventing boys from indulging in that most mischievous pastime or recreation of smoking cigarettes. It seems to me therefore that we already have sufficient legislation in that regard without asking this parliament to interfere. The proposition seems to me absolutely illogical, I say this with all due deference to my hon. friend, because it seems to me we are going further even than the premises of my hon. friend would logically carry him. I believe moreover that in this matter more can be done by domestic education than by legislation and that the way to treat a boy who 206J
has a cigarette in his mouth is to give him a good spanking.

I think the right hon. gentleman has overlooked one important factor in connection with the danger of cigarettes and tobacco. If I understand him correctly, he holds the opinion that the boy who smokes cigarettes is not more injuriously affected than if he smoked a cigar.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is my view.

If the tobacco were treated in both cases absolutely the same, I would say that that view might perhaps be correct. But the faet is that tobacco which is manufactured into cigarettes is treated with other narcotic poisons as well as nicotine, while tobacco made into a cigar is not so treated. For instance the tobacco used for the cigarette is often steeped in a solution of opium so that it has the same effect on the boy as the smoking of opium has on the Chinaman, or a solution of bel-ladona, which is an injurious narcotic poison. That is why, I believe, cigarettes are generally regarded as more injurious than tobacco or cigars. Whether the attention of the Prime Minister has been called to it or not that fact should not be left out of consideration. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bro-deur) express strong sympathy for the people who desire to prevent the manufacture of cigarettes. Their position reminds me of the story of the man who had no milk or food for his cat and felt so sorry for it that he petted it and sympathized with it and stroked it a great deal. The result was that the cat died, it needed milk, not sympathy. In the same way I feel it will be a long time before these reformers derive any benefit from the sympathy of these two ministers.
I have always understood that a unanimous expression of opinion by this House was practically a command to the government to enact legislation. A similar motion to that of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) was adopted two years ago and I believed that the government are in duty bound to take note of it. What are the government going to do ? As to whether or not this is an opportune time for the enactment of this legislation, the Minister of Inland Revenue says that this is only a Bill to change the Inland Revenue duty and it is not an opportune time to prohibit the manufacture of cigarettes. Could we not just as easily say by a clause of this Bill that cigarettes shall not be manufactured or sold as that the rate of duty on certain articles shall be charged. Did we not say that certain articles such as oleomargarine should not be manufactured in the country? By the same parity of reasoning this would be an opportune time to absolutely prohibit the sale of cigarettes as well as to

change the rate of taxation on them. If the government do not desire to go that far surely it is not too much to ask them to state to the House what their policy is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend has advanced a reason in support of this proposal which, if it is true, throws a flood of light upon this question. He has explained why the use of cigarettes is so deleterious, not only to boys but necessarily to mature men also. The reason is that it has been found in the army in Germany and in England that the use of cigarettes was deleterious. This is easily understood if it be true that in the preparation of cigarettes there is introduced not only tobacco but also such deleterious poisons as opium and belladonna. If it be true that there is placed upon the market and offered to the public for consumption a preparation containing opium and belladonna, then we know the cause of the evil and it is not difficult to apply the remedy, and the remedy should be to make a criminal offence to introduce certain deleterious substances into cigarettes or any form of tobacco. If it is true it is certainly a consideration which we should not overlook, this practice should be made an offence.
I have only to say that in the country of the right hon. minister's origin, it is stated in the medical works that it is an absolute fact and has been the custom for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In respect to the statement that cigarettes are adulterated by the introduction of poisons to strengthen the tobacco, within recent months complaints were made to the Inland Revenue Department to the effect that certain cigarettes were doctored up by the use of narcotics of some kind. A collection of -cigarettes was made, they were thoroughly analysed by Mr. McGill the chief analyst, and his report was made that there was nothing in the cigarettes save tobacco, he could find no other deleterious substance whatever.
That may be true with regard to the Canadian manufactured article, but of course I am not speaking as to that, I am speaking of the imported article.
Did he examine the paper ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It must be remembered that there are ten times as many Canadian cigarettes as imported cigarettes on the Canadian market. However, I shall have a further collection of cigarettes made and a very close examination conducted. I have often heard that the paper is so prepared that it is obnoxious. Possibly that is so and it may be that some cigarettes do contain a narcotic ; I know myself that they certainly have a different flavour.

The right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has stated Mr. SPROULB
that my position on this question is rather illogical. He states that the resolution which I had the honour of proposing, if carried by the House and legislation enacted embodying its principles, would prohibit altogether the use of cigarettes by all people in Canada. The right hon. gentleman himself forgot the point that a large portion of the cigarettes, the portion which we complain about, is used by boys under sixteen years of age. I believe that the grown up people of Canada, who wish to smoke their pipe or cigar and possibly some of them their cigarette, would be quite willing to forego any desire to smoke cigarettes in order to abolish this evil from the land in the Interest of the rising generation. The government have been taking one position in the House and another position in the country. Those of us who are interested in this question are confronted, on the one hand with the statement of some minister, and on the other hand, with the statement of some other minister in the country when they are engaged in elections. Let me give a reference to what the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) stated when this question was up in the House last session. In the discussion page 4077 of ' Hansard ' that hon. gentleman said:
It may be that the reason that these provincial and local laws are ineffective is that the provinces have not sufficient power to control the evil and that it is necessary, in order to control the evil that the law should he passed hy the supreme authority of the land, and should he equally effective and equally enforced and equally drastic all over the country. For this reason I would he temoted to support a resolution and a law on the lines herein indicated. I feel, however, that perhaps there has not been that fair effort on the part of the inferior powers in this country to accomplish the end.
Further on, when the discussion was closing, the Minister of Agriculture stated (page 4079 of Hansard) :
If my hon. friend should propose this motion in the early days of next session, before Christmas. I should he glad to do all I could to put through a measure which would prevent the use of cigarettes by young people. Therefore, unless my hon. friend should amend this motion so as to make it read next session instead of this, I cannot support it. I hope a Bill of this kind will be brought in next session and passed unless we can find other means more effective than those now in force to lessen this evil.
The Minister of Agriculture was speaking for the government as I understood him. He said, in order to get rid of the resolution for the time being, that he would be very glad next session to support a resolution along the lines of the resolution that I had up for discussion at that time and which was again debated in this House a few weeks ago. I regard this as an

important question. It is all very well for ministers of the Crown to stand up and say that they sympathize with this movement but the people of the country expected the government to face this question and' to legislate upon it. It is either right or wrong that the young people of Canada should smoke cigarettes and if the right hon. gf-utleman had the power to take the cigarette from a boy and chastise him upon the street in the city of Quebec, he would not fail in the greater duty which confronts him and his government. The right hon. gentleman must remember some of his ministers have stated that they are in favour of legislation of this kind, they have the power to put upon the statute-book legislation that will drive out this evil* and protect the youth of Canada and I- think it is the duty of the government to do that this session. We have been waiting for it since 1903. Long prior to 1903, when the Liberal-Conservative party were in power, all through the province of Ontario, the Women's Christian Temperance Union held meetings, passed resolutions, requested some candidates for parliament to make a pronouncement upon this question and gave expression to their belief that when the Liberal party came into power they would drive out all these evils which were such a burden on the hearts of the members of the Women's Christian Temperance Union particularly in the province of Ontario. It was the same way with regard to the liquor question - another moral question. The right hon. gentleman when in the city of Winnipeg, promised the people prohibition if the people voted for it and every province except Quebec voted in favour of it. Yet, the right hon. gentleman pushed it aside. Nothing has been heard of it since. They were going to abolish the bar in the House of Commons, and the hon. Minister of Agriculture the other day, in one of the provinces, stated that he never knew a bar was open in the House of Commons.
Oh, oh.

It was the Bar of Justice, I suppose, that he was referring to. We had this government coming into power, trying to carry out the pledges that they gave to the people on moral questions, and they suggested moving the bar from the House of Commons over to the Senate. Everybody knows that there is a bar in the House of Commons where you can get liquor. I am told they put a door keeper on the bar the other day to keep messengers out and let members of parliament, have more room I suppose. As to whether that is right or wrong, Mr. Chairman, I have nothing to say, and I only touch upon this question as it affects the great moral questions upon which pledges were given by the Liberal party when they were out of office and seeking the votes of the people. Now, they have been in office since 1896. In 1903 a resolution was introduced by a supporter of their own calling for the abolition of the manufacture and sale of cigarettes. That resolution was carried by a handsome majority. The Women's Christian Temperance Union and the supporters if this great moral movement went away perfectly satisfied. They said : Of course, possibly* the government will not have an opportunity at this moment to carry the resolution into effect by legislation, but at the next session of parliament it will be done. From 1903 down to this moment we have had nothing except resolutions discussed and statements from one minister or another to the effect that at the next session of parliament they will be glad to assist in placing upon the statute-book legislation prohibiting the manufacture and sale of cigarettes.
Now, when a minister of the Crown has a Bill touching this very question the government say : We are not ready to give any promise ; we have no policy, and they really have no policy except that stated by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bro-deur) who informs us that they have decided to put up the duty a little higher. The hon. gentleman suggests that possibly that will satisfy those who are in favour of legislation upon this subject. We expected an announcement to-day, and I may say that the right hon. gentleman will not satisfy his own friends, hundreds and thousands in number in every province, who believe that this is a great evil and that the time of parliament could not be better taken up than in discussing and placing on the statute-book something to drive out the evil. I pointed out in this House a few weeks ago that during the nine months ended March 31, 1907, there were 275.000,000 cigarettes consumed by the people of Canada. In so far as those were consumed by grown up people I have not very much to say. All I can say is that I believe that grown up people some of whom smoke cigarettes, would be quite willing to join hands with the government and to say that in the interest of their boys and girls and in the interest of the future of Canada they would be prepared to set that aside and confine themselves to the smoking of pipes and cigars. This is a golden opportunity which I expect the government to take advantage of in order to make a statement as to their policy upon this question. I do not suggest that they should legislate on it in connection with the Bill before the House, but what I do say is that they should make a statement to the people of Canada and the members of the cabinet who pledged their support to this proposition should see that

the government do something on the question. The people of Canada will not be satisfied with promises made occasionally in the House or on the hustings when a byelection is going on. But in view of the fact that a majority of this House in the session of 1903 voted in favour of the proposition and that a majority of the people of Canada are in favour of legislation on the question, it is the duty of the government to make plain to the people of Canada at this session what their policy is

whether it is in favour of legislation or is opposed to legislation. Then the people of this country will know what the position of the government is.
If I understand this legislation, its object is to do away with all distinctions, so that the purchaser will not know whether he is buying the product of the foreign leaf or the Canadian leaf.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The object of the legislation is to permit foreign tobacco and Canadian tobacco to be used together in the one factory and the one package, and there will be only one stamp which will indicate the tax paid.
Your imported raw leaf and Canadian leaf go into the same package, and you cannot tell by the label whether -the package contains mixed tobacco or foreign tobacco only or Canadian leaf only.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is the effect.
What is the object?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Its object is to permit the use of Canadian tobacco in all packages. One of the handicaps of Canadian tobacco has been the rebate of the duty when cuttings of foreign tobacco were exported. The factories using foreign tobacco could not use Canadian tobacco because we could not allow a rebate on the cuttings of Canadian tobacco. That was a great handicap on the use of Canadian tobacco. Another handicap was the stigma attached to the reputation of Canadian tobacco, which formerly was not so good as the imported, and the use of a distinguishing label kept up that stigma. But Canadian tobacco is greatly improved to-day and is susceptible of greater improvement, so that I do not think this handicap should be continued as it would be by our continuing the use of a special label. The great object is to have Canadian tobacco used in common with the tobacco of any other country in the same factory.

The minister says the object is to remove the handicap on Canadian tobacco. Would he have been equally as correct if he had said that the object is to remove the distinction between tobacco imported in the raw leaf and made in Canada and tobacco made from the Canadian ' Mr. BLAIN.
raw leaf? Would not that be equally specific and true? The minister admits that the opinion so far has been that the imported raw leaf is superior to the Canadian? By this legislation he is not only endeavouring to take away the handicap from the Canadian raw leaf but to give it the advantage in so far as that preference has to be considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I claim that Canadian tobacco has suffered serious disadvantage, and I want to remove that disadvantage.
I am not an authority on tobacco; but if any one is, it ought to be the minister. Is it his opinion that the Canadian is equally as good as the imported tobacco?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I would not claim that speaking generally, but I do claim that there is grown in Canada a considerable quantity of tobacco as good as any imported into Canada except the finer grades of Cuban tobacco. We know that there are great possibilities in Canada for the growth of good tobacco. The great question in the production of first-class tobacco is the harvesting of the crop and the curing of the weed. These are things concerning which our farmers have much yet to learn, but all the tobacco imported into Canada, whether in the manufactured state or in the raw leaf, is not good tobadco. There are many inferior cigars imported, and many of the Canadian cigars are better than even some of the imported cigars from Cuba.
Mi-. FOSTER. Of course we must compare equal grades. What I gather from the hon. gentleman is that in his opinion Canadian tobacco is not better than the imported. I am not personally interested, biit I know it is an objection to this legislation that you are obliterating the difference which absolutely exists and are trying to give an advantage to the Canadian product which it does not intrinsically possess. I am willing to go a fair distance in giving the Canadian product an advantage, but that may be carried a little too far. Has my hon. friend squared himself with the cigar manufacturers on the question of this one label? Have they not protested? I have a protest under my hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This legislation has been talked about for some time, and at first there was considerable opposition from the cigar manufacturers. That was largely due to the fear that the change in the colour of the labels would, in some way or other, affect their particular trade. They considered the label as indicating a particular brand, whereas all it proved is that the duty has been paid. But they have recently realized that their fears in that respect were groundless. We had delegations here repre-

senting the Hamilton and London Cigar-makers. Representatives of these firms stated that, if we did not by this legislation increase the duties paid, they had no objection to the adoption of one label. The manufacturers, generally, I think, take that view. To some extent, the cigarmakers- the workmen-have objected.
Have they withdrawn that objection ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, I cannot say so. That objection has come principally from the city of London. I have not heard much of it from Montreal or from cities west of London. These men say that by the use of Canadian tobacco, which, they say, is cheaper and inferior, a lower grade of cigars may be made that will be sold at prices less than the cigars they are making, and consequently the wages paid the cigarmaker will be smaller than those now paid. I must say I do not fear anything of that kind. Smokers choose cigars on their merits and not on the label.

I received this from one union :
We, the cigarmakers of Union 27, Toronto, strongly, protest against the alteration of stamps on cigars as being inimical to our interests as cigarmakers.
That is a sample of many that I have received. My object was to find out whether the minister had talked this matter over, and whether the union makers of cigars were fairly well pleased and had accepted their programme.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think that some of the union men in London and probably Toronto and other places have the view that the change to one label will affect the making of cigars. I think that many cigarmakers are quite satisfied, but the telegram read by die hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) shows that some are not.

The cigar that bears the black stamp may be made of Canadian tobacco provided they pay on the Canadian tobacco the same duty as would be paid on the foreign leaf. So the black stamp does not convey the assurance that it is a foreign leaf cigar.
I thought that the stamp showed which was the foreign leaf cigar.
Only the blue stamp.

Very well. But that blue stamp is to be done away with. Consequently, if I go into a store to buy a cigar I have to depend altogether on the merchant -I have to take his word. I am not a heavy smoker of cigars, though I smoke a little, and do not pretend to judge by the appearance of a cigar, but depend upon the stamp. Why do we in sending our apples abroad stamp them according to the grade, No. 1, No. 2, or No. 3? Is it not to protect the consumer? Our apples are to go to a foreign market, but the cigars we consume ourselves. I think the change is simply made for the purpose of forcing the Canadian consumer to smoke Canadian tobacco without giving them the means of knowing what it is they are buying. I have sympathy with everything Canadian and would be glad to assist in putting the Canadian leaf on the market, but at the same time if a man wants a foreign cigar he has a right to get it and to know what he is buying. London Is a very important place for the production of cigars. I believe it is the second largest in Canada. The hon. minister knows that what I say is correct.

Referring to section 13 of the Bill. I would like to know if the manufacturer, upon the payment of the rates and duties mentioned in the section, shall have the option of placing on said tobacco and cigars when offered for sale the uniform stamp?

I believe the change in the stamps is going to affect the cigar trade very much. The minister hardly puts it fairly. He knows that with the change to only one stamp any man who goes into a store who is not a good judge will have no idea of what he is buying. He cannot tell whether it is Canadian or partly or wholly foreign leaf.
It is the same to-day. The buyer of a cigar with a black stamp which would be supposed to be manufactured with foreign leaf may contain Canadian leaf.
There is a special stamp for the foreign.
No.
That is my understanding. There is a black stamp for the foreign cigar.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think not.

I have sympathy with the remarks made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie). It seems to me that the attempt in this Bill is to facilitate the sale of Canadian leaf as foreign leaf. If we are to encourage the use of Canadian leaf-and with that I am thoroughly in sympathy-I think it should be done openly and above board, and no advantage taken by a shuffling of the stamps which will confuse the consumer. I think the hon. member for London is right in saying that purchasers of cigars, as a rule, are guided by the stamp on the cigar, which stamps are supposed to indicate whether the cigars are of foreign or of domestic leaf. If the government wish-and I presume they do -to encourage the use of Canadian leaf, in my opinion the proper way is to do it openly by increasing the duty on imported

leaf, thus giving an advantage to the homegrown leaf in a proper and straightforward way. But that is not being done under this -Bill as I understand it.
The hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie) has stated that many men cannot judge at sight whether cigars are of foreign leaf or home leaf. It is too late, after a man has smoked a cigar, for him to say: Well, that was Canadian leaf and I bought it believing it was foreign leaf. He has smoked the cigar and found it was not up to the quality he expected, and makes his complaint afterwards. There should have been a proposition made by .the government, in my opinion that would have covered the case a little better than that, a proposition that would have been at the same time open and aboveboard. My suggestion would be that instead of raising the excise it should be left at 25 cents, and that the duty on the foreign leaf should be increased to 10 cents. That would make in all 35 cents, and would have given the home product an advantage in the duty which would have brought about I think an increased consumption in Canada of the home grown leaf. I am convinced that would be a right policy to pursue, and the government should not have endeavoured to bring it about by a shuffling of stamps so as to deceive the purchasing public. The public should understand what they are getting, but they cannot understand unless there is something on the box to indicate whether it is home or foreign leaf, or partly home and partly foreign. No change that will deceive the consumer is justifiable by the department. The government should increase the duty on the imported foreign leaf. That might increase the revenue also, and would place the article on its own merits before the people, and It would be left for them to say whether they were prepared to pay the higher price for the foreign leaf or to take the home grown at a lesser price. I believe that the view expressed by the hon. member for London will be the view of the large majority of cigar manufacturers in Canada, and I trust that the government will reconsider their proposition.

In my opinion the customs duty should have been raised and the excise should have been lowered. I never took the ground in the past, and never believed, that the use of one stamp only would benefit the grower to any extent; at the same time I cannot see where it is going to affect him in any way. So far as I am concerned I am prepared to buy cigars on their merits. So far as I know, I do not think any other country in the world brands their cigars as we have been doing.

We who represent counties where tobacco is grown do not look upon this measure as one intended to improve the growing of native tobacco, but as the removal of a grievance. I know of no other article which is stamped, as in this case,

with stamps of different colours. Our view was that the government, by putting a different coloured stamp upon the Canadian tobacco, encouraged the prejudice which for-many years existed against that article. There is no doubt that for many years there was not much improvement in the cultivation, the curing and the preparation of Canadian tobacco, on account of the prejudice existing against it. It was then probably that the different coloured stamps were invented; and now that the cultivation of Canadian tobacco has so greatly improved, we consider that the use of these different' coloured stamps is a grievance. I do not think the government was wrong in removing that grievance. It seems to me that the government is not called upon to indicate to the purchaser the kind of tobacco that he is buying. The object is to collect revenue upon a specific article; it is not the duty of the government to-indicate to the purchaser that he is buying Canadian or foreign tobacco, it is for the purchaser to assure himself of the quality.
I think the customs duty on foreign tobacco at the present time is high enough. The manufacturers or cigar unions who have protested against this measure, when they come to realize the object of the demands that have been made for a uniformity of stamps, will either withdraw, or at any rate diminish the force of their protest. I think it proper to make this statement, because this is a grievance which we have sought to have removed for more than fifteen years. I do not see that any valid reason has been given why we should brand, so to speak, the Canadian product with a specially coloured stamp which, under the circumstances I have indicated, is harmful to the industry.

I am glad to see that the Minister of Inland Revenue has taken this course with regard to these stamps.
I brought that matter before the House in 1903. A portion of the district I then represented, namely, the neighbourhood of Kelowna in the Okanagan district, grew a very excellent quality of tobacco, I think if not the best, at all events one of the best-qualities of tobacco grown in Canada. The soil there is particularly well adapted to the growing of good tobacco, and after the removal of this discrimination against Canadian tobacco as proposed by this Bill, I - think that industry will flourish and become important. I agree with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that the branding of Canadian tobacco with a green stamp, with the prejudice that existed against it, was a discrimination and a notice to all the world that it was an inferior tobacco that was being manufactured into cigars. After all, a man will smoke the cigar that he likes, whatever be the colour of the stamp. I am a smoker myself, and I think a fairly good judge of cigars, and I have found many imported cigars that I considered of inferior quality, and they are


not improving in late years ; although there are some cigars that are keeping up to the standard of their brands pretty well. I am glad to see that the Minister of Inland Revenue is proposing to abolish the discriminating and distinguishing stamp which I complained of in 1903.
Is it not a fact that in the United States they have a distinguishing stamp for imported cigars?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: So far as we know, they have but one stamp.

As bearing upon this question, I would like to read an article which I find in the Canadian Cigar and Tobacco ' Journal ' :
The only other demand is that the present regulations requiring separate factories for the production of this class of goods and separate, distinctive stamps for Canadian, combination and foreign leaf products he abolished, and the regulations so simplified with a single stamp and single license, as to permit the manufacturer to use Canadian tobacco in any desired manner.
It has been contended in the past that these regulations were necessary to prevent the public from being deceived as to what leaf was contained in the particular brand they purchased, and it is contended by the farmer that the practical result is to close the doors of nearly every factory in Canada to his leaf, and by the green and pink stamp to also put a badge of inferiority on his tobacco when it is offered to the prejudiced public.
Looking into the subject one is first confronted by the 'fact that no country in the world so stamps its own produce, and in the United States, to which we are always prone to turn for illustration, all tobacco products, whether made from American leaf, solely from foreign leaf, or from both in combination, one factory only is necessary, and only one revenue stamp is issued. Why, as a matter of plain common sense, should a manufacturer have to go to the enormous expense of equipping a separate factory and organization before he will be permitted to manufacture the product of his own country? To an impartial observer having no personal interest involved, the proposition seems as absurd as it is unjust. Every one in the trade knows only too well that this law has prevented the experimental use of Canadian tobacco in cigar factories and has effectively closed the doors of 235 cigar factories to the farmer who searches for a market for his crop. Little wonder then that no cigar leaf is grown in Canada to-day, when the factory door is closed to its use. There must necessarily be demand before there can be supply, and the market must be opened before iin-type of leaf will ever be grown in commercial quantity.
The other contention as to the necessity of green, pink and black stamps for the protection of the public seems equally hypocritical and absurd. Is Canadian tobacco more injurious to health that the public must be protected? One would almost think it was a poisonous article that must be labelled so that the public could discriminate and purchase
a non-poisonous article. Do we protect the public by a yellow stamp against the cigar made in a mold, and sold, by inference at Iqast, as hand-made goods? Do we, or should we, place a purple stamp on the clear Havana cigar to show its superiority over the seed and Havana product? Do we place a white stamp on the cigar made from American leaf, and which also reaches the public as a presumably Havana filled cigar? This solicitous interest in protecting the public cannot but bring a cynical smile to all familiar with the trade, and the time is ripe for us to discard such a hypocritical cloak. The consumer has an absolute protection in every cigar and every piece of tobacco he purchases, and that protection lies in the trade mark or brand under which it is sold. If the quality suits his palate, he purchases again, and factory regulations and separate stamps are quite unnecessary for his protection. Canadian tobacco will die out just as soon as it does not satisfy the public taste and it will increase in consumption just so far as it pleases the consumer. It is but fair that all handicaps should be removed from it, and it be given a clear field, free from triple factory obstruction and with reasonable protection to prove its worth. This freedom and this protection must necessarily precede and not succeed the demonstration of its worth. The law of supply and demand is arbitrary. The demand must precede the supply, and the conditions must be made favourable before the demand can be created.

You stated in that article that in the United States they do not designate the cigars made in that country by different stamps. As a matter of fact the stamps are entirely different both in colour and in shape ou an imported cigar and a domestic cigar.
It is not a different stamp on tobacco manufactured there.
Entirely different in colour and shape on a domestic and a foreign cigar.
You are referring to stamps on cigars manufactured in the United States and cigars imported.
The stamp on cigars manufactured in the United States is entirely different from that on imported cigars.

That is entirely different from this.

After obtaining the statements of opinion which I have just mentioned, Mr. Blaise Dugas proceeded to London, and Liverpool, England. There also he submitted to the inspection of experts the samples' of tobacco Mr. DUGAS.
which he had taken along with him. I shall quote herewith some of the evidence-thus obtained. The statement of Mr. Muller, of Messrs. W. O. Muller & Co., of London, is as follows :
The samples you are showing here are much better and would sell now if it was stripped, for London market, all tobacco must be sorted and stem taken out, sorted as to colour and size of leaves, 20 or 22 inches is considered good. No objections to larger leaves, colour brown, texture fine and strong appearance glossy and silky, packed when fermented and dry. In cases of 250 or 300.
In order to give your tobacco industry a. footing, it needs some organization controlled by planters or others. We have never seen Canadian tobacco before.

From the above I draw the conclusion that there is no reason to maintain the distinction made heretofore between Canadian tobaccos and foreign tobaccos in the matter of brands.
The paper from which I have quoted before recess makes the following further remarks, in an editorial dated October, 1905 :
Taking the primary query as to whether Canadian tpbacco has proven its claim as a marketable commodity, we can turn to no more conclusive evidence than statistics. In 1896, the fiscal year prior to the 10 cent tax on foreign leaf, we find that the manufacture of Canadian leaf amounted to only 590,283 pounds, and on referring to the returns for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1905, we see that 1,986,505 pounds of Canadian and combination tobacco have been made and sold. Comment is unnecessary, the figures completely answering the questions.
Admitting then that the slight protection granted in 1897 has resulted in this wonderful development and expansion of the Canadian tobacco consumption, the wisdom of the government's policy in imposing that tax in the interest of agriculture must be frankly admitted, despite the views held by practically all the trade at the time the tax was imposed. This trade opinion is now undergoing a complete change, in the face of the evidence steadily forcing itself upon all.
The question as to whether Canadian tobacco is improving in quality, and can undergo sufficient further improvement as to warrant prospects of still further increase in consumption in future and its ultimate use for cigar purposes, is a matter having important bearing on the issue, and is a speculative subject that can be reasoned only. by deduction. It is evident to all who have had an opportunity of inspecting and following the successive crops of tobaccos in western Ontario and Quebec, that they have improved materially in quality. This is due solely to the better knowledge gained by the farmer through practical experience in planting, cultivating, curing and handling his crop, and in view of the tobacco history of the world, it seems only fair to assume that this progress will continue and texture and quality of leaf be ultimately grown that will compare favour-ablv with such types of foreign leaf as those with which they are intended to compete.
The history of almost every type of leaf now popular in cigar and tobacco manufacture is practically the history that Canadian tobacco is now making. Sumatra was once a coarse, heavy, rank tobacco. Wisconsin was once inferior to the present Canadian cigar leaf. Connecticut is a story of complete evolution to its present fine texture and quality. Shade-grown Florida Sumatra has within the past three years passed from rank failure to marketable perfection. In the face of these facts, combined with proofs staring us in the face of what Canadian tobacco has already accomplished under the encouragement of a very meagre protection, can we any longer, as fair minded business men and loyal Canadians, decry the product of our own soil?
Is further protection now desirable and opportune? The farmer echoes an emphatic yes. Dried and fermented tobaccos. ' Dried tobacco which has not yet been subjected to fermentation no more deserves the name of smoking tobacco than unfermented grape juice deserves the name of wine.
In dried tobacco, the nicotine forms part of the organic composition of the plant, it becomes disengaged during combustion and emits strong and acrid fumes often of a disagreeable and repulsive odour.
On being subjected to fermentation, the dried tobacco undergoes important and radical changes which give it its full value.
Fermentation improves its tecture, colour, and flavour, makes it easier of combustion, and rids it of its acrid and biting flavour, its aroma becomes more marked but softer and finer. At the same time, the nicotine is partially eliminated and what remains is disengaged from the organic matter, so that fermented tobacco while more fragrant and perfumed, is really not so strong, and is pleasanter and healthier than dried tobacco.
Most agricultural products have to undergo fermentation before being fit for consumption : wheat flour, for instance, must be fermented with yeast before yielding good bread ; cheese is the product of fermented curds ; flax yarn is the product of flax fiber rotted that is to say fermented, &c., &c. Smoking tobacco worthy of that name, forms no exception to the rule, and we propose, in this study, to describe a rational method of fermentation employed in the United States and which deserves the best attention of our northern tobacco growers.
Our tobacco must therefore be put to the test of the curing, as the paper I have quoted explains. As may be seen, the intrinsic value of the product does not depend so much upon the cultivation of the plant ns upon the subsequent preparation it must undergo.
