And this afternoon, was the hon. gentleman in this House when the right lion, leader of the government, answering the remarks of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) relating to the prohibition of cigarettes, stated that he was not a smoker, and, speaking for himself, he would feel disposed to prohibit absolutely the use of tobacco in this country? Canada is perhaps afflicted with a prime minister too near to perfection. If he even did so much as to indulge in a smoke with a pipe or a cigar, we might have had that remedy sooner.
The hon. member for Montcalm this afternoon has found fault with the hon. leader of the opposition, because in 1901 and 1903 he protested against the heavy increase in the burden of taxation, giving as an illustration the duty on tobacco. Where does my lion, friend find in those .statements of the hon. leader of the opposition that he was opposed to a measure protecting the production of Canadian tobacco. If in 1901 and 1903, the hon. leader of the opposition complained of the increased taxation generally and of the duties on tobacco in particular, the only conclusion to be drawn from those statements is that a reduction of those duties would have fostered the industry which, according to the hon. member for Montcalm, is of such an import for this country.
My hon. friend (Mr. Dugas) has alluded to the experiment conducted by Mr. Goldstein, of Montreal. What has been the result? We do not know. The only thing wo know is that Mr. Goldstein is a staunch Liberal and from what was said by my hon. friend, I suppose that he has been given charge of 20,000 pounds of tobacco, and said that he was quite satisfied.
What has been said by the hon. gentleman about Mr. Blaise Dugas' trip in Europe establishes the merit of the suggestions made in this House since 1896, asking for the employment of experts from Connecticut to teach our farmers how to cure our tobacco for the European markets.
The verbal report-it has never been printed-of the agents sent in Wisconsin by the government was never followed with any practical result, and has been totally ignored.
I have congratulated the hon. Minister of Agriculture for having secured the services of Mr. Charlan, who has furnished valuable information on that industry. But, as I have said the other day, until we become experts in the way of packing, curing and shipping tobacco, we cannot expect to have a profitable market for this product.
If five or six million pounds of tobacco will answer the demand for home consumption, it is quite obvious that if our produc-

tiou reaches fifty million pounds we must find an outlet for the surplus, and up to this date the government has done nothing in that direction.
Therefore, it ill becomes the hon. member for Montcalm when hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are opposing this measure to find fault with those who for many years before him had been advocating the interests of this industry.
On the question : Shall the preamble be adopted ?

May I ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) what he would think of a proposal to prohibit the importation of cigarettes into Canada ? If the government are not prepared to make a statement on the main question as to the total abolition of the manufacture and sale of cigarettes, what would my hon. friend think of a proposition to prohibit the importation into Canada of cigarettes ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid the proposition is hardly involved in the Bill before the committee and I would not care to offer an opinion on the subject in this manner.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
Bill (No. 135) to amend the Immigration Act.-Mr. Oliver.
Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 113) to amend the Land Titles Act.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would briefly explain the objects of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The object of this Bill is to provide for the holding of land in the interest of church organizations in the Northwest, or in that part of the country where the administration of the rights in regard to land is in the hands of this parliament. At the present time there is no provision for the holding of church rights by any organized body in that territory ; so that, it is desirable that there should be legalized the holding of church rights which must be especially legalized by Act of parliament in all that part of the territory which is outside of the Yukon, and by special Act of the Yukon legislature within the Yukon Territory. The circumstances are such that it wopld be right and proper that a general provision should be made that would apply to all cases and
that would govern the holding of church property according to the terms of this Bill. It has no application except in what is called the Northwest Territory and the Yukon Territory.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1-lands belonging to churches and congregations-
In the case of a church that has a bishop, would this enable trustees or a congregation to hold lands, or would it be incumbent upon them to pass it over to the bishop?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: According to the wording of this section there is an alternative right. The bishop may hold the church property, the congregation may appoint trustees to hold it.
Suppose that according to the rules of the church the bishop only can hold the property and the congregation desire it to be held by trustees, whose authority would then prevail?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If it is the rule of the church that the property should he held by the bishop and not by trustees, the Act would give the bishop the necessary legal authority to hold it. The Act also provides that in the case of those churches which have no bishop, the property may be held by the congregation or by the trustees of the congregation.
Does the Land Titles Act apply to the different provinces of the Northwest or only to the Northwest Territories outside of the organized provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To the territory which is called the Northwest Territory, which is outside of the organized provinces, but including the Territory of the Yukon.
But it does not apply to Saskatchewan and Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. Those provinces pass their own laws with regard to land titles.
But you handle the land, and when you sell or homestead it don't you give a title to that land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but as soon as the land passes into the hands of private owners all further transactions with regard to it are subject to legislation of the provinces under them jurisdiction over property and civil rights.
When you sell or give [DOT]away the land, don't you give a title to it under the Land Titles Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We give a title, but that title has to be registered under the Land Titles Act of the province for use in future transactions.

Do you not give a deed of the land under the Land Titles Act which we are dealing with here? Is there one Land Titles Act for the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and different ones for Saskatchewan and Alberta ?

If I understand this Bill, its purpose is to provide that in the territories outside of any province, where a bishop already holds land on behalf of his church, or where trustees of a congregation hold land on behalf of their church, upon their ceasing to hold office or dying, instead of the property going to their heirs or being in the clouds, it goes exofficio to the next bishop or to the trustees appointed in succession to the previous trustees without any conveyance.
I was asking if the same rule applied to the new provinces.
When the Crown gives & patent to a piece of land that patent is taken by the party to whom it is given to register it under the Land Titles Act of the province.
The Land Titles Act, as it is in the revised statutes, is, I presume, intended to apply to all Dominion lands wherever they are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It will apply to all Do-(min'ion lands until they pass from the Crown. There is no title to those lands until they have passed from the Crown. This Bill is to apply to lands which have passed from the Crown in the Territories which have no local government handling the Land Titles Act.
This Act applied to Saskatchewan and Albert until they were set apart as provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The difficulty I find is that there is no application defined in the Act. It is simply called a Land Titles Act, and we must conclude that when it was passed it applied to all lands over which the government had control and could not apply to any lands belonging to any of the provinces. This is an amendment to the Land Titles Act, and I presume could not apply to any property which has been acquired from the Dominion government in any territory which has become organized by the establishment of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Any land already vested in any church in those provinces is not controlled by this amendment.

There is one point I would like explained. The amendment says :
123a. The bishop of any church, or any trustees for any church, or any congregation of any church, holding land for the purpose of such church or congregation shall respectively, with regard to such land and any dealings therewith, be deemed to be a body corporate and politic

That is the first statement. Then it goes on to say:
-and land so held shall devolve respectively upon the successors in office of such bishop or upon the successors in office of such trustees duly appointed in manner by law or by such church or congregation prescribed.
It repeats that the land shall be held by the successor in office of such bishop or by the successors in office of such trustees, but it does not refer in any way to any congregation or church.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am advised that the congregation does not cease to exist as do trustees or as does a bishop. The congregation continues without intermission, and therefore there is no need to provide that there shall be successors to the congregation.

The congregation being a continuous body is a reason why there is no provision as to their successors in office ; but there being no provision in this amendment for the devolution of property from a congregation, why mention the congregation at all ?

Whoever drew this Bill wanted to provide for the case where there were no trustees. If the property was vested in the members of a congregation as such, and some of them died, the estate might pass to the heirs at law. This Bill purports to make them a body corporate and politic, so that when a member of the congregation dies or retires, and his successor comes in, the title at once passes to his successor.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

Bill (No. 142) to amend the Bills of Exchange Act.-Mr. Aylesworth-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object of this section is to correct what, I apprehend, has been simply a printer's error in the Bills of Exchange Act as it appears in the present revised

statutes. It lias been the law for many years, as this statute, when first passed declared, that any holder of a promissory note or bill of exchange who endorses it, by the act of endorsing it>
precludes himself from disputing certain things with regard to the bill or note-precludes himself, for instance, from denying the genuineness of the bill or the regularity of its drawing and the genuineness of the signatures that were upon it when he so endorsed it. But it was not as against the wide world that he, by endorsing, precluded himself from malting these denials ; it was only as against men to whom that negotiable i>aper might subsequently pass. That is to say a man who endorsed a bill of exchange or promissory note by his act of so endorsing it closed his own mouth against the possibility of ever afterward saying that that bill was not a genuine bill so far as the men who took it from him or relying upon his signature were concerned. Accordingly the provision of the Bills of Exchange Act previous to the revised statutes, was that the endorser of a bill by endorsing it is precluded from denying to his immediate or a subsequent endorsee that the bill was, at the time of his endorsement, a valid and subsisting bill and that he had a good title thereto. By some error the word ' endorsee ' is printed ' endorser '-the final ' e ' is made an ' r,' and, accordingly, the law for the last fourteen months has been that a man by endorsing a bill of exchange precluded himself from denying, not to those who came after him, but to his immediate or subsequent endorser-if one can understand what that phrase means-that the bill was genuine and that he had a good title to it. It is a pure misprint, so far as I can understand. No one had thought of changing the law that has been the established law for many years, and it is to restore it to what it was prior to this revision of the statutes that I am proposing to change the word from ' endorser ' to ' endorsee,' which it was as the Bill was passed fifteen years ago.
If there was anything irregular, the redress would be against the original maker, I suppose ?

I understand clearly that this Bill does not in the least change the law as to bills of exchange as the law has been held by the courts in the past. The object is merely to get rid of a printer's error. We all know that there have been most intricate questions about this doctrine as to how far a man adopts signatures on bills of exchange, and it would be very dangerous if any attempt were made in an Act of parliament, without very grave consideration, to alter the law as it has been interpreted by the courts in the past. I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) to say that there is no intention to alter what the courts have held in the past on this subject, but merely to make the statute conform to the former holdings of the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) understands the situation exactly. This Bill is hot to change the law at all, but to restore what has been the law, always I may say, this amendment being necessary because the law was inadvertently changed in the revision of the statutes by a printer's error.

Do I understand the minister to say that he knows, as a matter of fact, that the statute from which this was revised was as it is now proposed to make the law read ? I recollect the law as being the same as the minister says it was, but I also assume that the minister has looked back to see that the statute from which the revision was taken was in the form which he suggests now-that the word was ' endorsee,' not ' endorser.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am restoring the condition that existed prior to the revision. When my attention was called to this error, I at once went back to the original Bills of Exchange Act and found that the word there was ' endorsee,' and had always remained ' endorsee ' until the new revised statutes were struck off, when it was printed ' endorser '-I imagine purely by a printer's error.
I asked the Minister of Justice a question. I do not know whether he thought it worth while to deign to reply to it or not, but I would like an answer before the Bill passes.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) would state the question again.

The question is this : Suppose that the original maker did not pay the bill and the endorser was obliged to pay it because of his endorsation, and suppose that the contention was set up that the bill was an illegal one, could the endorser, having paid it, have recourse against the original maker and the people who collected it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section does not touch that question at all. This merely relates to the effect of a man endorsing. The effect is to close that man's mouth against disputing the genuineness of the bill which he has endorsed-it closes that man's mouth so far as those who come after him, and whose title, therefore, depends upon his signature, are concerned, but not as to other people. It does not affect one way or the other the principle of law which has been referred to, that the endorser may fall back upon the maker, just as one en-

dorser may fall back on those who have gone before himself.
I asked the other question because I presumed the Minister of Justice Would be a competent authority to give us the status of the endorser.

I understand my hon. friend's question is as to whether this amendment will affect the rights to which the endorser of the Bill would have to proceed against the original maker. I understand the Minister of Justice states that this Bill does not affect these rights in any way; it only deals with the status of the endorser and the subsequent party into whose hands the Bill may come.
I asked in addition the question what rights the endorser would have to collect from the original maker, I am asking what the law would be.

The Minister of Justice suggests to me that the law remains-as it always was in that respect, and that the man who puts his name on the back of a bill as an endorser or the party who eventually pays the bill to any person who may be the holder, always has recourse against the original maker, and that right is not affected.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
Bill (No. 144) to amend the Winding-up Act-Mr. Aylesworth-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
I have been looking at the amendment and at the original Act, and I am not able to discover much difference. The word 'taking' is put for the word 'making,' otherwise they seem to be the same.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object of the Bill is to make clear beyond peradventure what the law is. This legislation is suggested by the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal of Manitoba, who, notwithstanding the interchange of one or two letters on the subject between himself and the Department of Justice, continues to feel, as he says, considerable doubt. This Bill is not intended to make the slightest change m the law, but to make, the law perfectly clear. It has been for many years the law under the Winding-up Act that the beginning of the winding-up of a company supersedes any execution which may be outstanding against the company, unless that execution has been completely carried out by the payment of the money over to the execution creditor. That being the law, when this section came to be re-enactetd in the re-Mr. AYLESWORTH.
vised statutes it was divided into two subsections, and provided, just as the Bill now under consideration provides, first, for the case of an execution placed In the hands of the sheriff against the real or personal property of the company, and next for the case where the property of the company is seized by way of an attachment, or by the registering of a memorial, or by making a garnishee order. The section as printed in the revised statutes is divided into two subsections, and making the first subsection as it were an independent provision by itself, possibly not depending as it was of course intended to depend, upon whether or not the execution has been completely carried out by payment of the money, but apparently an absolute declaration that no charge on the property should be created by delivery to the sheriff of any execution, or by seizure or levy by the sheriff upon the property of the company. So it makes, as it were, a distinct enactment that under the Winding-up Act you could not create a lien upon the property of a company by issuing an execution and the shevi ff seizing. The true interpretation of the section, as it stands in the revised statutes to-day, is, I think, that it is only where there Is a winding-up, and the winding-up actually begun before the levying under execution is completed, that tiie law declares the issuing of the writ should not create a lien or charge upon the property. But the possibility that doubt might arise as to the interpretation of the section is the reason for seeking to make the law abundantly clear. As I say, one learned judge at any rate tells me that he finds great difficulty about it, that it seems like an absolute declaration of the law, as it stands in the revised statutes, that the issuing of an execution against the property of the company does not create any lien or privilege upon that property in favour of the creditor. The section in the amended Bill now under consideration has simply been recast in such a manner as to make it abundantly plain that what the law is declaring is that no lien or privilege is created by putting an execution against a company into the sheriff's hands unless, before the winding-up begins, that execution is completely carried out and the money paid over.

I think I understand the object now. But there is another point I call attention to. In the revised statutes we have the words ' or by the issue or making of any attachment or garnishee order or other process,' and in the new statute we have the word taking ' instead of the word ' making,' ' or by the issue or taking of any attachment.' Is the word 'taking' intended to be used or is it a mere accidental change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the word has been changed to * taking ' advisedly. In the revised statutes it was declared that no lien or privilege should be created upon

the property of the company by the issue or making of any atachment or garnishee order. The word ' making ' is now changed to ' taking,' I think advisedly, as I find the word ' taken ' at the end of the subsection. The phrase might be changed by putting in the word ' out ' after ' taking.'
That would be an improvement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
